name: message-dispatcher
intent: Put one coordinating component in front of a channel so that it dequeues each message and hands it to exactly one performer, letting several consumers on a single channel process messages concurrently under an explicit, centrally controlled dispatch policy.
problem: Several consumers must serve one channel, but the assignment cannot be left to the messaging infrastructure: some messages need a specialized performer, others only need a performer that is currently free, and the application wants to decide, observe, throttle or trace that choice. When the consumers also share expensive per-performer state (a connection, a warm cache, a session), handing the dequeue decision to the infrastructure makes the assignment invisible and untunable.
context: In-process, server-side message consumption where the channel and its consumers live in the same runtime: an event-driven consumer or a dequeue loop reads a channel and the application fans the work out to a pool of workers. Applies when performer selection is a real decision (specialization, affinity, fairness, per-performer limits) and a coordinator is cheap; once the deployment uses a broker that already assigns messages to consumers (competing consumers in a consumer group, partitioned queues), the dispatch decision usually belongs to the broker and the in-process dispatcher only decides what happens inside one consumer.
benefits: The dispatch policy lives in one place: round-robin, least-busy, affinity by key, specialist selection or per-performer rate limiting can be changed without touching a single performer.
Performers become simple and uniform - they receive a message and process it - so they can be pooled, replaced or scaled independently of the channel they serve.
Per-performer setup (connections, caches, sessions) is amortized over many messages instead of being paid per message or hidden inside the infrastructure.
Dispatch is observable and steerable: the dispatcher is the natural seam for tracing, metrics, fairness, admission control and back-pressure before work starts.
Concurrency is bounded and tunable in one place, instead of being an emergent property of how many consumer instances the infrastructure happens to start.
tradeoffs: The dispatcher is a single point of contention and failure: every message passes through one dequeue-and-assign step, so a stalled or crashed dispatcher starves all performers, and throughput is capped by that step rather than by the number of performers.

It does not scale out the way competing consumers do: the coordinated dequeue lives in one process, so adding machines does not add dispatch capacity, and the pattern gives up the broker's built-in load balancing across instances.

Dispatching changes delivery semantics: by taking over the hand-off the application also takes over acknowledgement, retry and duplicate suppression, so at-least-once delivery and idempotency become design responsibilities that the pattern does not solve for you.

Queue bounds decide the failure mode: an unbounded queue converts overload into memory growth, while a bounded queue needs a rejection policy (block, reject, drop, caller-runs) that callers must understand.

Shared mutable state across performers, per-thread assumptions and resource ownership (who closes the connection the performer borrowed?) become visible hazards exactly because the assignment of work to worker is now application logic.

participants.responsibility: Consumes messages from the channel, selects exactly one performer per message and hands the message over; owns the queue bounds, the dispatch policy and the failure semantics of the hand-off.
Processes a single message handed to it by the dispatcher and delegates the rest of the work into the application; may be newly created or reused from a pool.
Keeps performers alive and bounded (thread pool, worker goroutines, virtual threads, process pool), so dispatch costs neither thread creation nor per-message setup.
Encapsulates the selection rule - round-robin, least-busy, affinity by message key, specialist by message property - so performers stay unaware of why they were chosen.
The event-driven consumer or dequeue loop that supplies messages to the dispatcher; keeps the channel's acknowledgement, ordering and back-pressure contract.

use_cases: A JMS/AMQP listener inside one application process that must fan each incoming message out to a bounded thread pool, with a queue bound and a rejection policy chosen by the application.

A server that hosts warm per-worker state (database connections, caches, model handles) and wants messages assigned to the worker that already holds the right state instead of whichever consumer the broker picked.

A workload where some messages must be routed to a specialized performer (a slow writer, a GPU worker, a compliance-checked handler) while the rest go to a general pool - the channel stays one channel, the decision stays local.
Per-key ordering or affinity: messages from the same entity must be processed by the same performer, so a dispatcher hashes the key to a performer while still running many performers in parallel.
Fair sharing between tenants or request classes when the transport offers no priority or quota, implemented as a dispatch policy with per-performer limits and pacing.
A single-consumer transport (a file tail, a database queue table polled by one poller) that must still be processed by many workers.

Apache Camel's SEDA component is an in-process staged route: a BlockingQueue separates producers from consumers, concurrentConsumers bounds the worker side, and queue-full behavior can be made explicit for an asynchronous hand-off.

Akka Typed's Pool Router creates a fixed set of routees and forwards each message to one routee (round-robin by default), making bounded local performer selection explicit; use a Group Router when routees are discovered across a cluster.

Spring Integration's ExecutorChannel uses a UnicastingDispatcher and TaskExecutor for asynchronous point-to-point hand-off, with configurable load balancing and failover; because the sender returns before the handler, transaction and acknowledgement boundaries must be explicit.
avoid_when: The transport already implements competing consumers (JMS message-driven-bean pools, Kafka consumer groups, SQS consumers, cloud queue triggers): the broker's dequeue assignment is the dispatcher, and rebuilding it in-process adds a hop, a bottleneck and a second failure domain.

Performers are equivalent and stateless, and the only goal is throughput: competing consumers scale across machines while a dispatcher cannot; a plain submit to a thread pool per message is simpler than a dispatcher object.

The choice of consumer depends on the message content (type, customer, region): put a Content-Based Router or Datatype Channel upstream so the routing decision is a topology fact rather than hidden application code.

Exactly-once, ordered or transactional processing is required: the pattern hands you the acknowledgement boundary without solving it; a transactional client or a broker-managed queue with the guarantees you need is the honest choice.
A single consumer already keeps up, or the work is not message-shaped: no coordination need exists, and a queue of one is just overhead.
anti_patterns: The dispatcher that also performs the work: once the coordinator processes messages itself, the roles collapse and the dispatch step becomes the bottleneck it was meant to remove.
Creating a performer per message with no bound, so that a burst turns into unbounded thread/goroutine/task creation and the dispatch policy degenerates into "whoever starts first".
An unbounded submission queue advertised as elasticity: overload is absorbed as memory growth until the process dies, and no caller ever learns that the performers cannot keep up.
A dispatcher that owns business logic, transaction boundaries and retry policy at the same time, becoming a god-object that no performer can be tested or reasoned about without.

Re-implementing Message Dispatcher on top of a broker that already offers competing consumers, or on top of a framework that already dispatches (MessageListenerContainer, ActorSystem, DispatchQueue), and paying for two coordinators.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: the decision which performer serves a message is separated from processing the message.
Single responsibility per role: the dispatcher dispatches, performers perform, the policy decides.
Open/closed principle: new dispatch policies and specialized performers plug in behind the selection seam without changing the channel or the other performers.
Explicit coupling: the hand-off point (queue, acknowledgement, failure handling) is a named, observable place rather than an implicit property of a transport.
Bounded resources: concurrency and queue depth are configuration of one component, not an emergent effect of infrastructure behaviour.
best_practices: Keep exactly one owner of the dequeue step per channel, and let that owner only assign work - never process it.
Bound the queue and choose the at-bound behaviour deliberately (block, reject, drop, caller-runs); make the choice visible to callers.
Keep performers interchangeable: inject the message, not the channel, and avoid shared mutable state so any performer can serve any message unless the policy says otherwise.
Define the failure contract of the hand-off explicitly - acknowledgement point, retry, dead-letter destination, duplicate handling - and implement it in the dispatcher.
Reuse performers through a pool when per-performer setup is expensive, and tear the pool down deterministically on shutdown (drain, then cancel stragglers).
Instrument the dispatch step (queue depth, wait time, per-performer occupancy, rejection count) because it is the single place where the whole flow can be understood.
Prefer the transport's own competing consumers when the performers are stateless and equivalent; keep an application-level dispatcher for the decisions the transport cannot make.
sources: Hohpe, G. & Woolf, B., Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Message Dispatcher (Messaging Endpoints chapter); Competing Consumers in the same chapter is the contrasting solution.
